extracted.intended_audience: members of the public, stakeholders, and petitioners interested in participating in FTC rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for members of the public on how to participate in Federal Trade Commission rulemaking (notice-and-comment and Section 18 proceedings), including what to include in comments, how to petition for rulemaking, and participation opportunities at different stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to the notice with reference to proposed text and agency reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically, FTC rulemaking involves publishing a notice with the proposed text of the rule. The notice explains the agency’s reasoning for the proposal and asks the public to submit comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base your comment on the notice and the proposed text; explain how the proposed text would work in practice or why it should be changed. The agency asks for public comments specifically in response to its reasoning and proposed language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include substantive information: data, experiences, perspectives, or arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: An effective comment gives additional information, data, experiences, perspectives, or arguments, but it doesn’t need to be long or formal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete evidence, empirical data, real-world examples, or reasoned arguments to support your position. Short, focused comments with substantive content are appropriate; avoid purely rhetorical statements without supporting facts or reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address specific questions posed in the notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Often, the FTC’s notice will ask specific questions about the proposed rule and its effect. A comment addressing one or more of those questions is particularly helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the notice's questions and structure responses to them. Direct answers to posed questions help the agency evaluate specific impacts, alternatives, and tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: You may submit comments on behalf of yourself, a group, or a business
rubrics_metrics.description: You can submit a comment on behalf of yourself, a group, or a business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When commenting for an organization or business, clearly state your affiliation or representational capacity. Comments can reflect individual experiences or collective viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participate at the three Section 18 stages: ANPR, NPR, and informal hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: In Section 18 rulemakings you have three opportunities to weigh in by responding to an Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking; responding to a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking; and presenting your views at an 'informal hearing,' if a hearing is held and you request to speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor each stage and submit input at whichever stage is most appropriate for your information (early-stage conceptual input at the ANPR, detailed reactions to proposed text at the NPR). If an informal hearing is held and you wish to speak, request to participate in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rebuttal comments and cross-examination for specific factual disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: During the rulemaking process, commenters with specific factual disputes about the rule may submit rebuttal comments or conduct cross-examination at informal hearings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you contest factual claims submitted by others or by the agency, file rebuttal comments that cite evidence. If an informal hearing allows cross-examination and you need to challenge another party's factual assertions, request the hearing and be prepared to identify the disputed facts and supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: File a petition for rulemaking when FTC has not issued a notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC accepts and reviews petitions for rulemaking from the public. If you file a qualifying petition with the FTC, it will be posted for members of the public to provide comments about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the Procedures for Addressing Petitions in the Code of Federal Regulations when preparing a petition. A properly filed petition can prompt a formal rulemaking and will be opened to public comment once posted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find and use official sources: Federal Register and Title 16 CFR
rubrics_metrics.description: For access to the FTC’s rulemaking notices, visit the Federal Register. To find existing FTC rules, visit Title 16 of the Code of Federal Regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Federal Register to locate current notices and the CFR (Title 16) to review existing rules and regulatory text referenced in notices. Citing precise references (docket numbers, rule text locations) in comments improves clarity.
